name: DragonRank

Malware families such as PlugX and BadIIS
Web shell indicators on IIS directories
DLL side‑loading artifacts in AppLaunch.exe or certutil usage
Suspicious file path placement like "Kaspersky SDK" directories
Exploitation of known CVEs (e.g., CVE‑2024‑9047, CVE‑2025‑31324)
Remote Desktop Protocol usage with stolen credentials
SQL injection triggers in web apps
Malicious IIS native modules deployed on public servers
Use of legitimate security tools for persistence and concealment
keyCapabilities: Deploy web shells on Windows IIS servers
Exploit public-facing application vulnerabilities (e.g., WordPress, phpMyAdmin, CVE‑2024‑9047) to drop shells
Install malicious IIS native modules (fashttp.dll, cgihttp.dll) for SEO hijacking
Launch BadIIS or PlugX backdoors for persistence and credential dumping
Use DLL sideloading via legitimate binaries (AppLaunch.exe, certutil)
Perform lateral movement using RDP, WMI, and stolen domain accounts
Escalate privileges via cloned admin accounts or local account manipulation
Conceal malware by obfuscating file paths and altering attributes
Gather system information via web shell discovery scripts
Run black‑hat SEO campaigns for third‑party clients
recommendedActions: Monitor IIS host configurations for unauthorized dlls (fashttp.dll, cgihttp.dll) and modules
Implement regular integrity checks on website directories and IIS installation folders
Block known malicious domains and IPs linked to BadIIS, PlugX, Cobalt Strike, and mail.tttseo.com
Enforce least‑privilege RDP policies; enable MFA for remote access
Patch public web applications (WordPress, phpMyAdmin) promptly and harden server configurations
Detect and filter SEO poisoning patterns via SERP monitoring tools
Deploy endpoint detection on IIS servers to flag DLL sideloading and PowerShell stagers
Segment networks to isolate web servers from core infrastructure
Monitor for abnormal registry edits linked to RDP manipulation or scheduled tasks
Educate security staff to recognize black‑hat SEO and malicious domain activity
campaignsText: DragonRank’s campaigns exhibit a high degree of automation and scripting. Operators set up scheduled tasks to sustain persistence, modify registry entries for RDP manipulation, and establish HTTP/WS tunnels as C2 channels. The actor consistently exploits well‑known vulnerabilities in public web applications, deploys web shells, and then rolls out backdoors for credential harvesting and lateral exploitation. Campaigns are often carried out from multiple command servers, frequently using Tor or custom domains to obfuscate traffic. Victims include mid‑size enterprises and government agencies with publicly exposed IIS services; the group typically pivots to more critical assets once a foothold is secured. The operational tempo appears quarterly to biannual, with periods of heightened activity when new vulnerabilities become public.
description: DragonRank is a financially motivated Chinese‑speaking threat actor that chiefly targets public‑facing Windows IIS servers across Asia and Europe to deploy web shells, hijack SEO traffic, and exfiltrate credentials and data. The group leverages both publicly known application vulnerabilities and malicious IIS modules such as BadIIS, while maintaining persistence with PlugX and other backdoors for lateral movement and credential harvesting. Continuous, script‑driven operations combine black‑hat search engine manipulation with sophisticated post‑exploitation techniques that keep attackers in the network long after initial compromise.
goals: DragonRank’s strategic objectives are twofold: first, to monetize compromised infrastructure by monetizing search engine traffic through SEO poisoning and redirecting victims to gambling or other illicit sites; second, to accumulate valuable credential material and exfiltrate sensitive data for resale or future exploitation. The actor’s broad sector coverage reflects an opportunistic approach aimed at maximizing revenue generation from any network that can be weaponized as a high‑traffic web host. By maintaining persistent footholds via PlugX and BadIIS, DragonRank can stay ahead of defensive measures, making it possible to extend operations beyond the initial compromised server into core business services such as finance or telecommunications, where financial gains or strategic intelligence are most lucrative.
